Acceptance summary:

In this study, the authors examined the function of the RNA-binding protein FPA through analyzing its protein interactome and its global impact on gene expression using a combined approaches of Nanopore DRS, Helicos DRS, and short-read Illumina RNA-Seq. The combined datasets and new computational approaches developed by the authors showed a predominant role of FPA in promoting poly(A) site choice. The authors further revealed that FPA mediates widespread premature cleavage and polyadenylation of the transcripts of NLR genes, which act as important plant immune regulators. Overall, this study suggests that control of transcription termination processes mediated by FPA provides an additional layer of the regulatory dynamics of NLRs in plant immune responses.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article “Widespread premature transcriptiontermination of Arabidopsis thaliana NLR genes by the spen protein FPA” for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Hao Yu as the Reviewing Editor and Detlef Weigel as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Chae Eunyoung (Reviewer #1); Blake C Meyers (Reviewer #3).

Essential Revisions:

While there was agreement that the topic is timely and the findings relevant, there were some concerns regarding manuscript structure, inconsistency among some results, and interpretation of biological relevance of the data, as listed below, that need to be addressed to support the conclusions.

1. The manuscript presents an extensive body of studies in analyzing FPA interacting proteins and its potential RNA targets including NLRs. Although the overall results cover a series of observations, many of them are descriptive and divert the audience's attention from understanding the novelty and significance of the findings. Thus, we suggest that the authors re-organize the manuscript into a more coherent story and focus on the most important data pertaining to NLR control as shown in the title and the abstract.

2. The authors should address or explain some inconsistencies in the results as mentioned by reviewers. For example, the authors found that at least for some pathogens, "loss of FPA function does not reduce plant resistance". This is not consistent with the hypothesis that FPA is important for regulating NLR immune response genes, and the observation that premature exonic termination of RPP7 caused by FPA has a functional consequence for Arabidopsis immunity against Hpa-Hiks1.

3. The significance of this study will be strengthened by analysis of the biological relevancy of the alternative polyadenylation events mediated by FPA pertaining to NLR functions. We suggest that the authors consider either providing new experimental data or clearly interpreting existing results, such as those relevant to regulation of RPP7, to provide better insights into biological significance of the data presented in this manuscript.

Please also take into consideration the other specific comments from the reviewers below to revise the manuscript.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript by Parker and colleagues presents an extensive body of work on characterizing the role of FPA in the choice of polyadenylation sites in transcripts of A. thaliana. Investigation on the mechanistic details that FPA engages on the mRNA processing was first initiated with the in vivo pull-down followed by LC-MS/MS, which revealed the its protein interactome relevant for 3'-end processing. The main dataset pertaining to the manuscript title comes from the comparative transcriptome analysis of Col-0, fpa-8 mutant and the overexpressor of FPA, 35S:FPA:YFP. The strength of this work lies in the use of nanopore DRS by demonstrating the layers of FPA-dependent transcripts, including its own, and its comparison to datasets by Illumina RNA-Seq and Helicos DRS. The systematic analysis uncovered unexpected complexity in the A. thaliana NLR transcriptome under the control of FPA and thus delivers a new insight on NLR biology. Several studies anecdotally have reported the importance of using genomic DNA, but not a single cDNA species, for addressing full functionality of NLR genes. Recent advances in NLRome sequencing from multiple genomes of a species and NLR structure/function studies also highlight the importance of understanding modular nature of NLR. As alluded with the modular diversity of NLRs kept in the genomes of a species in recent studies, NLR genes are prone to reshuffle in the genome to generate different variants, including partial entities with the loss of some parts of the proteins or even chimeras, supposedly maximizing the repertoire for defense. This work adds the level of transcript diversity on that of genomic diversity; FPA, an essential factor for transcription termination determinant, targets numerous NLRs to control the layers of NLR transcriptome of an individual plant. Although it is yet to be clarified for the regulatory significance of FPA-mediated NLR transcript changes under biotic or abiotic conditions, the authors succeeded in employing fine genetic schemes utilizing FPA-defective vs. -overexpressing lines along with long-read nanopore DRS technology for the first time to uncover the breadth of differential transcript generation focused on 3'-end choices. This work is timely and impactful for NLR research owing to the above-mentioned recent advances in NLR field.

As this work is the first of its kind in utilizing nanopore DRS to address NLR transcriptome, several technical concerns can be addressed to corroborate the claims made in the manuscript, which authors can find in the following section (1-8). Regarding the organization of the manuscript, the authors may consider to rebalance the two parts: FPA interactome vs. FPA targets and NLRs. Overall, the manuscript can be seen as combining two stories; first to characterize FPA function in 3'-end processing of transcripts inferred by interacting proteomes and meta-analysis of ChIP-seq data; second part includes detailed analysis of NLR transcripts and others. Although the first half of the analysis is a necessary prelude to the following NLR analysis, the current title and academic novelty mainly lies, or were intended by the authors, on the NLR analysis. However, current manuscript has relatively enlarged section of the first with NLR analysis packed into a series of supplementary dataset. If authors wishes to opt for highlighting NLR analysis, the following suggestions would help (9-14).

1) Earth mover distance (EMD) has been applied to identify a locus with alternative polyadenylation. What is the basis of using EMD value of 25 as a cutoff? According to Figure 4 B,D, EMD can range from 0-4000. One would also wonder if the distance unit equals bp.

In addition, EMD values of some genes (e.g. FPA and representative NLRs) can be specified in the main dataset so that significance of the cut-off values shall be appreciated.

2) Regarding the manual annotation of alternatively polyadenylated NLR genes (L1160-):

Genes with alternative polyadenylation were identified and the ending location was supported when there were minimum four DRS reads. It would be relevant to provide the significance of "the four" based on read coverage statistics, for example, with average read number covering an annotated NLR transcript with the specification of an average size.

3) Figure 4E shows that Ilumina-RNAseq dataset detects the number of loci with a different order of magnitude compared with the other two methods. Reference-agonistic pipeline shall be appreciated, however, the method engaged might have elevated the counting of paralogous reads mapped to different locations than they should be. Along with paralogous read collapsing, this is always a problem with tandemly repeated genes, such as NLRs by and large. For example, NLR paralogs in a complex cluster with conserved TIR/NBS but diversified LRRs would have higher coverage in the first two domains but drop in the diversified parts. The authors need to specify their bioinformatic consideration to avoid such problems.

Although the tone of the Illumina read section was careful and the main 3'-end processing conclusion was made by nanopore DRS, the authors are also advised to clearly state the limitation of using Illumina-RNAseq to address alternative polyadenylating sites at the beginning of the section, for example what to be maximally taken out from Figure 4 E and 4F. This will give relative weights to each dataset generated by different methods. One advantage of using Illumina data would be that the expression level changes can be associated with changes in processing, it seems.

4) At the RPP7 locus, At1g58848 is identical in sequences with At1g59218 as is At1g58807 with At1g59214 (two twins in the RPP7 cluster by tandem duplication). It would be good to check whether the TE At1g58889 readthrough indeed occurs in the sister duplicate with a potential TE in the downstream of At1g59218. If not, it can be used as an example of duplication and neofunctionalization through an alternative polyadenylation site choices.

5) HMM search shall be revisited to confirm if they are to detect the TIR domain. Given that a large proportion of NLRs in A. thaliana carry TIR at their N-terminal ends and the specified examples included TIR-NLR, it is surprising to see no TIR domain in Figure 5.

6) L659-668: how does the new data relate to the previously TAIR annotated At1g58602.1 vs At1g58602.2 (Figure 6, Inset 1)? It would be good to see these clearly stated in the main text as compared to newly identified ones. From the nanopore profiling, At1g58602.2 appears to be the dominant form.

7) One thing to note is that in the overexpressor of which Hiks1 R is suppressed, there was hardly any At1g58602.1 produced in addition to the large reduction of At1g58602.2. Thus, relative functional importance of the two transcripts shall be discussed in line with the Hpa resistance data. Accordingly, L740-741 phrasing shall be revised to include the possibility of absolute or relative "depletion" of functional transcript(s) contributing to the compromise in Hpa resistance.

8) It would be necessary to state in the main text the implication of phosphorylation on the two Ser residues on Pol II at L245. A clear description distinguishing the effect of the two phosphorylation and the specificity of the antibodies is desirable, as the data was interpreted as if the two sites made differences, such that Ser2 was heavily emphasized (e.g. subtitle). Albeit low level, Ser5 data also shows an overlap with FPA ChIP-seq coverage at the 3' end. If there is a statistical significance to be taken account to interpret the coverage, please state it. Given that elongation occurs progressively, I wonder how much should be taken out from the distinction.

9) Figures presentation for RPP4 and RPP7 are great in detailing the FPA-dependent NLR transcript complexity. To make the functional link more evident, the authors may consider bringing up parts of the Figure 5-supplement to a main Figure to detail the revised annotation of NLRs. Given recent advances in NLR structure and function studies, extra domain fusion, fission and truncated versions of NLRs require a great deal of attention. For example, potential functional link to the NMD-mediated autoimmunity and revised annotation of At5g46470 (RPS6) needs a clear visual guidance preferably with a main figure (Figure 5-Sup3).

10) The section "FPA controls the processing of NLR transcripts" includes dense information and can be broken down to several categories. To this end, Supplement File 3 (NLR list) shall be revised to deliver the categorical classes and further details and converted to a main table.

For NLR audience, for example, it would be important to associate the information to raw reads to assess where the premature termination would occur. At least, the ways to retrieve dataset or to curate the termination sites shall be guided.

On the contrary, there is no need to include other genes in Figure 4-Figure Supplement 4-8 under this section. They are not NLRs.

11) Figure 7 and IBM1 section can be spared to supplement.

12) The list of "truncated NLR transcripts" in particular, either by premature termination within protein-coding or with intronic polyadenylation, should be made as a main table. The table can be preferably carrying details in which degree the truncation is predicted to be made. With current sup excel files, it is difficult to assess the breadth of the FPA effect on the repertoire of NLRs and their function. This way, functional implication of differential NLRs transcriptome can be better emphasized.

13) FPA-mediated NLR transcript controls, as to promote transcript diversity, is expected to exert its maximum effect if FPA level or activity is subject to the environmental stresses, such as biotic or abiotic stresses. The discussion on effectors targeting RNA-binding proteins (L909-918) is a great attempt in broadening the impact of this research. In addition, if anything is known to modulate FPA activity, such as biotic or abiotic stresses or environmental conditions, please include in the discussion.

14) NLR transcript diversity as source of cryptic variation contributing to NLR "evolution" is an interesting concept, however, evolutionary changes require processes of genic changes affecting transcript layers or stabilizing transcriptome diversity. In the authors' proposition in looking into accessions, potential evolutionary processes can be further clarified.

Reviewer #2:

Parker et al attempted to show that the FPA protein functions to regulate the widespread premature transcription termination of the Arabidopsis NLR genes. Using in vivo interaction proteomic-mass spectrometry, FPA was shown to co-purified with the mRNA 3' end processing machinery. Metagene analysis was used to show that FPA co-localized with Pol II phosphorylated at Ser2 of the CTD heptad repeat at the 3' end of Arabidopsis genes. Using a combination of Illumina RNA-Seq, Helicos, and nanopore DRS technologies, FPA was found to affect RNA processing by promoting poly(A) site choice, and hence controls the processing of NLR transcripts whereas such process is independent of IBM1.

Overall, it is a potentially important research. The data is rich and could be useful. However, the biological stories described are not thoroughly supported by the data presented, especially when the authors tried to touch on several aspects without some important validations and strong connections among different parts. Some special comments are provided below:

(1) The title of this manuscript is "The expression of Arabidopsis NLR immune response genes is modulated by premature transcription termination and this has implications for understanding NLR evolutionary dynamics". Therefore, the readers will expect some functional connections between the FPA and the novel NLR isoforms due to premature transcription termination. However, the transcript levels of plant NLR genes are under strict regulation (e.g. Mol. Plant Pathol. 19:1267). Since the functions of NLR genes are related to effector-triggered immunity, it is more important to study the function of FPA on premature transcription termination when the plants are challenged with pathogens. In this manuscript, most transcript analyses are based on samples under normal growth conditions. It is therefore a weak link between the genomic studies and the functional aspects. For instance, it is more important to identify unique NLR isoforms produced upon pathogen challenges that are regulated by FPA. The authors will need to provide some of these data to fill this gap.

(2) Since the function of FPA is to regulate NLR immune response genes, we should expect a change in plant defense phenotype in FPA loss-of-function mutants. Could the authors provide more information on this? On the contrary, in line 728 of this manuscript, the authors found that at least for some pathogens, "loss of FPA function does not reduce plant resistance". It is not consistent with the hypothesis that FPA is important to regulate NLR immune response genes.

(3) Furthermore, the authors mentioned in lines 729-731 "Greater variability in pathogen susceptibility was observed in the fpa-8 mutant and was not restored by complementation with pFPA::FPA, possibly indicating background EMS mutations affecting susceptibility." Does it mean that fpa-8 contains other mutations? Will these additional mutations complicate the results of the RNA processing? Could the authors outcross the fpa-8 mutation to a clean background?

(4) In line 318, the authors found 285 and 293 APA events in the fpa-8 mutant and the 35S::FPA:YFP construct respectively, but only 59 loci (line 347) exhibited opposite APA events (about one fifth). The low overlapping frequency suggests that some results could be false positive.

(5) In line 732-736: "In contrast, 35S::FPA:YFP plants exhibited a similar level of sporulation to the pathogen-sensitive Ksk-1 accession (median 3 sporangiophores per plant). This suggests that the premature exonic termination of RPP7 caused by FPA has a functional consequence for Arabidopsis immunity against Hpa-Hiks1." It is contradictory to the statement in line 728 that "loss of FPA function does not reduce plant resistance". Is it possible that overexpression of FPA:YFP had generated an artificial condition that is not related to the natural function of FPA?

(6) The fpa-8 mutant has a delayed flower phenotype (Plant Cell 13:1427). Could the 35S::FPA:YFP fusion protein construct reverse this phenotype and the plant defense response phenotype? It is important to interpret the data when the 35S::FPA:YFP construct was used to represent the overexpression of FPA.

(7) Under the subheading "FPA co-purifies with the mRNA 3' end processing machinery". The results were based on in vivo interaction proteomics-mass spectrometry. MS prompts to false positives and will need proper controls and validations. Have the authors added the control of 35S:YFP instead of just the untransformed Col-0? At least for the putative interacting partners in Figure 1A, could the authors perform validations of some important targets, using techniques such as reverse co-IP, or to show direct protein-protein interaction between FPA to a few of the important targets by in vitro pull-down, BiFC, or FRET, etc.

(8) In Fig. 3, the data show that the last exon of the FPA gene is missing in the FPA transcripts generated from the 35S::FPA:YFP construct. Will the missing of this exon affect the function of the transcript and the encoded protein?

(9) The function of FPA is still ambiguous. There was a quantitative shift toward the selection of distal poly(A) sites in the loss-of-function fpa-8 mutant and a strong shift to proximal poly(A) site selection when FPA is overexpressed (35S::FPA:YFP) in some cases (Fig. 3, Fig. 5, Fig. 8). But the situation could be kind of reversed in other cases (Fig. 6). What is the mechanism behind it?

(10) Under the subheading: "The impact of FPA on NLR gene regulation is independent of its role in controlling IBM1 expression". IBM1 is a common target of FPA and IBM2. Indeed, FPA and IBM2 share several common targets (Plant Physiol. 180:392). It may be more meaningful to compare the impact of FPA and IBM2 on NLR gene instead.

(11) In lines 423-425, the authors described "Consistent with previous reports, the level of mRNA m6A in the hypomorphic vir-1 allele was reduced to approximately 10% of wild-type levels (Parker et al., 2020b; Ruzicka et al., 2017) (Figure 4-figure supplement 3)." This data could not be found.

(12) In line 426: "However, we did not detect any differences in the m6A level between genotypes with altered FPA activity." Which data this statement is referring to?

Reviewer #3:

In the article "Widespread premature transcription termination of Arabidopsis thaliana NLR genes by the spen protein FPA", the authors describe the function of FPA as a mediator of premature cleavage and polyadenylation of transcripts. They also focused their study on NLR-encoding transcripts, as that was their most novel observation, describing an additional layer of control.

In general, the article is well written and clear. The experimental design is good, they didn't seem to over-interpret the results, the controls were solid, and the nanopore data were quite informative for their work. It is rather descriptive maybe bordering on dry in parts - but the results will be helpful for those working on NLRs, and demonstrate the utility of bulk long-read transcript data. The authors were able to string together a number of descriptive observations or vignettes into an informative paper. Overall, it is solid science, but maybe not monumental.

One minor complaint is that the authors don't focus on NLRs starting on line 436, and then they have extensive results on NLRs; by the time I got to the discussion, I'd forgotten about the early focus on the M6A. While the first part of the article is necessary, I would suggest a more concise results section to give the paper more focus on the NLR control (since that is emphasized in the abstract and the title of the manuscript).

[Editors' note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Widespread premature transcription termination of Arabidopsis thaliana NLR genes by the spen protein FPA" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Detlef Weigel (Senior Editor), Hao Yu (Reviewing Editor) and three reviewers who reviewed the last version of the manuscript.

We feel that this revised manuscript has been significantly improved, but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as indicated in the following comments given by Reviewers 1 and 2.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors made great efforts to reorganize the manuscript to address comments from all three reviewers. Current manuscript supports the main claim on FPA modulating the NLR regulation with a series of graphic illustration as main figures with supporting supplements. These encompass the breadth of regulatory roles of FPA on different NLR genes, in particular. Their quantitative assessment of the FPA effects on clustered or hypervariable NLR genes have been performed in a sound way, taking on the latest research outcomes (2020-2021 publications) on NLR diversity and evolution.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, it is a piece of interesting research supported with rich data. The authors have addressed much of the concerns in the revised version and through further explanations. Some remaining questions could be addressed via clarification, strengthened comparison, and additional discussions.

1. In relation to my original Question 1. Since the title of this manuscript is "Widespread premature transcription termination of Arabidopsis thaliana NLR genes by the spen protein FPA" and some NLR gene expressions are responsive to pathogen attack, the readers may be interested to know the changes in NLR genes under pathogen attack conditions that are regulated by FPA. If the authors have these data, it will be great to share.

2. In relation to my original Question 2 and Question 5. Since overexpression of FPA only partially reduces the level of functional RPP7 transcripts, is it possible that FPA overexpression also acts on other NLR transcripts that leading to loss of resistance?

3. In relation to my original Question 4. Is it possible to make a comparison directly between the 35S::FPA:YFP line versus the fpa-8 mutant to investigate see whether all disappeared pre-mature transcriptional terminations have returned to the level of Col-0 or even more?

4. In relation to my original Question 6. The authors showed that overexpression FPA will decrease the overall FLC transcripts. Is the FPA acting on the pre-mature transcriptional termination of FLC too? Any data to support this?

5. In relation to my original Question 7. Does the anti-FPA chip data match well with the proximal APA in Col-0?

6. In relation to my original Question 9 and Question 10. IBM1 is a common target of FPA and EDM2, indicating the possible coordination of the FPA and EDM2 functions. There have been several studies on EDM2, could the authors compare the target of FPA and EDM2, and also address whether FPA also targets TEs in introns of function genes similar to that of EDM2?

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

I am satisfied with the authors' response to the reviewers, including the valuable points raised by the other reviewers. The extensive changes that the authors made to the manuscript have substantially improved the work.

claims.source: Pol II Ser2 was enriched at the 3′ end of PIF5 in Col-0 but depleted from this region in fpa-7 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: FPA autoregulates its expression by promoting premature cleavage and polyadenylation within intron 1 of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010).
claims.source: FPA autoregulates its expression by promoting premature cleavage and polyadenylation within intron 1 of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010.

claims.claim: A proximal poly(A) site in the first intron and distal sites in the terminal intron and exon of FPA could be mapped in Col-0 using Nanopore and Helicos DRS.
claims.source: Consistent with this, a proximal poly(A) site in the first intron and distal sites in the terminal intron and exon of FPA could be mapped in Col-0 using Nanopore and Helicos DRS (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A quantitative shift towards selection of distal poly(A) sites in the loss-of-function fpa-8 mutant and a strong shift to proximal poly(A) site selection when FPA is overexpressed was detected using all three data types.
claims.source: Using all three data types, we detected a quantitative shift towards selection of distal poly(A) sites in the loss-of-function fpa-8 mutant and a strong shift to proximal poly(A) site selection when FPA is overexpressed (35S::FPA:YFP).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from Illumina RNA-Seq, Helicos DRS, and Nanopore DRS.

claims.claim: Using Nanopore DRS, 285 and 293 loci with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively, were identified.
claims.source: Using this approach on Nanopore DRS data, we identified 285 and 293 loci with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 77.9% (222) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in fpa-8 displayed a positive change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a predominant shift to distal poly(A) site selection.
claims.source: In all, 77.9% (222) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in fpa-8 displayed a positive change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a predominant shift to distal poly(A) site selection (Figure 2B, left panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 56.7% (166) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP displayed a negative change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a shift towards proximal poly(A) sites.
claims.source: In contrast, 56.7% (166) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP displayed a negative change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a shift towards proximal poly(A) sites (Figure 2B, right panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 16 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) site selection in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) site selection in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=3.9 × 10−7).
claims.source: A total of 16 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) site selection in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) site selection in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=3.9 × 10−7), demonstrating that loss of function versus overexpression of FPA can result in reciprocal patterns of poly(A) site choice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data.

claims.claim: Using Helicos DRS, 319 and 299 genes with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively, were identified.
claims.source: We used the same approach to identify loci with FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation in Helicos DRS data. We identified 319 and 299 genes with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: The predominant shifts in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP were towards distal (79.0% or 252 loci) and proximal (75.3% or 225 loci) poly(A) sites, respectively, as detected by Helicos DRS.
claims.source: Consistent with Nanopore DRS analysis, the predominant shifts in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP were towards distal (79.0% or 252 loci) and proximal (75.3% or 225 loci) poly(A) sites, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: 44 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) sites in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=4.8 × 10−30) as detected by Helicos DRS.
claims.source: In all, 44 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) sites in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=4.8 × 10−30), again demonstrating reciprocal poly(A) site selection depending on FPA activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Helicos DRS data.

claims.claim: Of the 222 loci identified with shifts to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 using Nanopore DRS, 39.6% (88) were also detected using Helicos DRS.
claims.source: Of the 222 loci identified with shifts to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 using Nanopore DRS, 39.6% (88) were also detected using Helicos DRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 44.0% of loci (73) with proximal polyadenylation detected in 35S::FPA:YFP using Nanopore DRS were also detected using Helicos DRS.
claims.source: Likewise, 44.0% of loci (73) with proximal polyadenylation detected in 35S::FPA:YFP using Nanopore DRS were also detected using Helicos DRS.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Nanopore and Helicos DRS data.

claims.claim: Using Illumina RNA-Seq, 2535 loci with differential RNA processing events in fpa-8 were identified: 1792 were upregulated, 390 were downregulated, and 353 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (FDR < 0.05, absolute logFC >1).
claims.source: Using this approach, we identified 2535 loci with differential RNA processing events in fpa-8: 1792 were upregulated, 390 were downregulated, and 353 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (FDR < 0.05, absolute logFC >1; Figure 2F, left panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: 1747 loci with differential RNA processing events were identified in 35S::FPA:YFP: 997 were upregulated, 532 were downregulated, and 218 had both upregulated and downregulated regions.
claims.source: A total of 1747 loci with differential RNA processing events were identified in 35S::FPA:YFP: 997 were upregulated, 532 were downregulated, and 218 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (Figure 2F, right panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: FPA does not influence global levels of mRNA m6A methylation.
claims.source: However, we detected no differences in the m6A level between genotypes with altered FPA activity. Therefore, we conclude that FPA does not influence global levels of mRNA m6A methylation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of m6A/A ratios.

claims.claim: Only 10.6% of loci with altered poly(A) site choice in 35S::FPA:YFP have altered H3K9me2 in ibm1 mutants compared with 14.2% of all loci tested (hypergeometric p=0.97).
claims.source: When we analysed two independent ChIP-Seq datasets of H3K9me2 in ibm1–4 mutants (Inagaki et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2020), we found that only 10.6% of loci with altered poly(A) site choice in 35S::FPA:YFP have altered H3K9me2 in ibm1 mutants compared with 14.2% of all loci tested (hypergeometric p=0.97; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-Seq data from Inagaki et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2020, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: FPA-dependent poly(A) site choice is not an indirect consequence of FPA control of IBM1.
claims.source: This result suggests that FPA-dependent poly(A) site choice is not an indirect consequence of FPA control of IBM1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis of H3K9me2 ChIP-Seq data in ibm1 mutants.

claims.claim: Sequences encoding NB-ARC, Rx-like coiled coil (CC), and/or LRR domains were enriched amongst the loci with increased proximal polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.source: We found that sequences encoding NB-ARC, Rx-like coiled coil (CC), and/or LRR domains were enriched amongst the loci with increased proximal polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The TNL gene AT5G46490, located in the RPS6 cluster, is incorrectly annotated as two loci, AT5G46490 and AT5G46500.
claims.source: For example, we found that the TNL gene AT5G46490, located in the RPS6 cluster, is incorrectly annotated as two loci, AT5G46490 and AT5G46500 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: AT5G46490 is actually a single locus with a previously unrecognised 2.7 kb intron containing a proximal poly(A) site, the use of which is controlled by FPA.
claims.source: Nanopore DRS evidence indicates that this is actually a single locus with a previously unrecognised 2.7 kb intron containing a proximal poly(A) site, the use of which is controlled by FPA.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data.

claims.claim: The 3′UTR of RPS6 is complex, with multiple splicing events and poly(A) sites.
claims.source: Nanopore DRS indicates that the 3′UTR of RPS6 is complex, with multiple splicing events and poly(A) sites (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: An independent unannotated gene that overlaps the RPS6 3′UTR was detected.
claims.source: We also detected transcripts expressed from this region that do not appear to be contiguous with RPS6 3′UTR reads. Instead, these reads correspond to an independent unannotated gene that overlaps the RPS6 3′UTR.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data.

claims.claim: The unannotated gene overlapping RPS6 3′UTR encodes a TIR domain similar to that of RPS6.
claims.source: The gene encodes a TIR domain similar to that of RPS6 (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by protein alignment shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data.
claims.source: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data; of these 124, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation (Tables 1–3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: Of the 124 expressed NLRs, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation.
claims.source: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data; of these 124, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation (Tables 1–3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: Of the 74 expressed NLRs located in major clusters, 44 (59.5%) were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02).
claims.source: Of the 74 expressed NLRs located in major clusters, 44 (59.5%) were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02) (Lee and Chae, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data and a citation to Lee and Chae, 2020.

claims.claim: 20 (71.4%) of the 28 expressed NLRs reported to be under high levels of diversifying selection were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02).
claims.source: Consistent with this, 20 (71.4%) of the 28 expressed NLRs reported to be under high levels of diversifying selection were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02) (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data and a citation to Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021.

claims.claim: FPA-sensitive NLRs tended to be located in regions with higher levels of synteny diversity, although the association was not significant (t-test p=0.09).
claims.source: In addition, FPA-sensitive NLRs tended to be located in regions with higher levels of synteny diversity (Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020), although in this case the association was not significant (t-test p=0.09; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synteny diversity data from Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation is associated with rapidly evolving NLRs.
claims.source: Overall, these findings suggest that FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation is associated with rapidly evolving NLRs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the association of FPA-sensitive NLRs with major clusters, high diversifying selection, and synteny diversity.

claims.claim: For 17 NLR genes, a change in FPA activity altered the formation of readthrough or chimeric RNAs containing one or more NLR loci.
claims.source: For 17 NLR genes, we found that a change in FPA activity altered the formation of readthrough or chimeric RNAs containing one or more NLR loci (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: The duplicated RPP7a/b-like genes AT1G58848 and AT1G59218 displayed increased readthrough into downstream transposable elements (TEs) in fpa-8.
claims.source: The duplicated RPP7a/b-like genes AT1G58848 and AT1G59218 (which form part of the RPP7 cluster containing five CNL-class NLRs) displayed increased readthrough into downstream transposable elements (TEs) in fpa-8 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The TNL-class gene AT1G63730, located in the B4/RLM1 cluster, forms chimeric RNA with the downstream TNL-class gene AT1G63740 in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 1099, FDR = 0.02).
claims.source: For example, the TNL-class gene AT1G63730, located in the B4/RLM1 cluster, forms chimeric RNA with the downstream TNL-class gene AT1G63740 in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 1099, FDR = 0.02; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 17 NLR genes with intronic polyadenylation controlled by FPA were identified.
claims.source: We identified another 17 NLR genes with intronic polyadenylation controlled by FPA (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: A proximal poly(A) site within the third intron of AT1G69550 results in mRNAs with a premature stop codon; the encoded protein lacks most of the predicted LRR domain.
claims.source: For example, we identified a proximal poly(A) site within the third intron of AT1G69550, which encodes a TNL-type singleton NLR (Figure 4B). Use of this poly(A) site results in mRNAs with a premature stop codon; the encoded protein lacks most of the predicted LRR domain.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In fpa-8, readthrough at the proximal poly(A) site in AT1G69550 is increased (Helicos EMD = 1271, FDR = 1.2 × 10−4), resulting in an increase in the relative number of full-length transcripts.
claims.source: In fpa-8, readthrough at this poly(A) site is increased (Helicos EMD = 1271, FDR = 1.2 × 10−4), resulting in an increase in the relative number of full-length transcripts.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: 45 NLRs were controlled by premature termination within exons.
claims.source: The most common form of FPA-dependent NLR regulation was premature termination within exons (Table 3). We identified 45 NLRs controlled in this way: at 44 of these loci, termination occurred within protein-coding exons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: At RPP28 (AT2G14080), multiple exonic poly(A) sites located within the second and fourth exons were detected.
claims.source: For example, at RPP28 (AT2G14080), which encodes a TNL-class singleton NLR, we detected multiple exonic poly(A) sites located within the second and fourth exons, which encode the NB-ARC and LRR domains, respectively (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Selection of exonic poly(A) sites at RPP28 was increased in 35S::FPA:YFP (Helicos EMD = 859, FDR = 5.4 × 10−9) and decreased in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 912, FDR = 7.6 × 10−9).
claims.source: Selection of these exonic poly(A) sites was increased in 35S::FPA:YFP (Helicos EMD = 859, FDR = 5.4 × 10−9) and decreased in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 912, FDR = 7.6 × 10−9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: At RPP13 (AT3G46530), FPA overexpression causes selection of proximal poly(A) sites located within the region encoding the LRR domain (Helicos EMD = 228, FDR = 1.8 × 10−4).
claims.source: For example, at RPP13 (AT3G46530), which encodes a CNL-class NLR protein, FPA overexpression causes selection of proximal poly(A) sites located within the region encoding the LRR domain (Helicos EMD = 228, FDR = 1.8 × 10−4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: At AT5G40060, FPA-dependent proximal polyadenylation in the region encoding the NB-ARC domain results in a transcript containing only the uORF, which is not a predicted NMD target and may be more efficiently translated into a TIR-only protein.
claims.source: Therefore, FPA-dependent proximal polyadenylation in the region encoding the NB-ARC domain results in a transcript containing only the uORF, which is not a predicted NMD target and may be more efficiently translated into a TIR-only protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from Nanopore DRS data and knowledge of NMD targeting.

claims.claim: In seven of the identified genes, exonic proximal polyadenylation is associated with retention of an upstream intron.
claims.source: In seven of the identified genes, exonic proximal polyadenylation is associated with retention of an upstream intron (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: RPS4 was previously shown to be regulated by alternative splicing induced by the effector AvrRps4 (Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
claims.source: For example, the TNL-type NLR RPS4 was previously shown to be regulated by alternative splicing induced by the effector AvrRps4 (Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang and Gassmann, 2007.

claims.claim: An increase in RPS4 intron 3 retention in 35S::FPA:YFP compared with Col-0 was associated with proximal polyadenylation events in exon 4 (Helicos EMD = 34, not significant).
claims.source: We identified an increase in RPS4 intron 3 retention in 35S::FPA:YFP compared with Col-0 that was associated with proximal polyadenylation events in exon 4 (Helicos EMD = 34, not significant; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: RPP4 (AT4G16860) is a TNL-class NLR known to mediate Arabidopsis resistance to Hpa isolate Emoy2 (Hpa-Emoy2) (van der Biezen et al., 2002).
claims.source: One example is RPP4 (AT4G16860), a TNL-class NLR known to mediate Arabidopsis resistance to Hpa isolate Emoy2 (Hpa-Emoy2) (van der Biezen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van der Biezen et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In wild-type Col-0, RPP4 can be transcribed as a chimeric RNA together with the downstream AtCOPIA4 TE (AT4G16870) through selection of one of the two distal poly(A) sites located within the TE (Wang and Warren, 2010).
claims.source: In agreement with a previous study (Wang and Warren, 2010), we found that in wild-type Col-0, RPP4 can be transcribed as a chimeric RNA together with the downstream AtCOPIA4 TE (AT4G16870) through selection of one of the two distal poly(A) sites located within the TE (Figure 5; Wang and Warren, 2010) or selection of a third poly(A) site in the downstream gene AT4G16857.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 5 and a citation to Wang and Warren, 2010.

claims.claim: Use of the proximal poly(A) site within the TE is associated with an approximately 8 kb cryptic splicing event between the 5′ splice site of the first exon of RPP4 and a 3′ splice site located within the TE.
claims.source: Use of the proximal poly(A) site within the TE is associated with an approximately 8 kb cryptic splicing event between the 5′ splice site of the first exon of RPP4 and a 3′ splice site located within the TE.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS and Illumina RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: The cryptic splicing event at RPP4 skips all RPP4 exons downstream of exon 1, removing most of the RPP4 coding sequence and introducing a stop codon.
claims.source: Both Nanopore DRS and Illumina RNA-Seq data provide evidence for this cryptic splicing event, which skips all RPP4 exons downstream of exon 1, removing most of the RPP4 coding sequence and introducing a stop codon (Figure 5, Inset 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS and Illumina RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5, Inset 1.

claims.claim: The cryptically spliced RPP4 transcript is predicted to encode a TIR-domain-only protein.
claims.source: The resulting transcript is predicted to encode a TIR-domain-only protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the Nanopore DRS data showing the cryptic splicing event.

claims.claim: Loss of FPA function decreases chimeric RNA formation at RPP4 by shifting poly(A) site selection towards a proximal poly(A) site located within the protein-coding region of the final exon.
claims.source: Loss of FPA function decreases chimeric RNA formation by shifting poly(A) site selection towards a proximal poly(A) site located within the protein-coding region of the final exon (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In 35S::FPA:YFP, increased selection of a proximal poly(A) site located within the first intron of RPP4 was observed, which would also encode a truncated RPP4 protein.
claims.source: Furthermore, in 35S::FPA:YFP, we observed increased selection of a proximal poly(A) site located within the first intron of RPP4, which would also encode a truncated RPP4 protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data.

claims.claim: RPP7 encodes a CNL-class NLR protein which is necessary for resistance to Hpa isolate Hiks1 (Hpa-Hiks1) in Col-0 (McDowell et al., 2000).
claims.source: RPP7 encodes a CNL-class NLR protein which is necessary for resistance to Hpa isolate Hiks1 (Hpa-Hiks1) in Col-0 (McDowell et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McDowell et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The full-length expression of RPP7 is controlled by elongation factors that interact with H3K9me2, which is associated with the COPIA-type retrotransposon (COPIA-R7) located in RPP7 intron 1 (Saze et al., 2013).
claims.source: The full-length expression of RPP7 is controlled by elongation factors that interact with H3K9me2, which is associated with the COPIA-type retrotransposon (COPIA-R7) located in RPP7 intron 1 (Saze et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saze et al., 2013.

claims.claim: At least two poly(A) sites within the COPIA-R7 element in RPP7 intron 1 were identified, both of which were selected more frequently in fpa-8.
claims.source: Using Nanopore and Helicos DRS data, we identified at least two poly(A) sites within the COPIA-R7 element, both of which were selected more frequently in fpa-8 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Two poly(A) sites within the second intron of RPP7 were identified, the use of both sites is reciprocally sensitive to FPA activity, with a moderate decrease in fpa-8 and an increase in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.source: We also identified two poly(A) sites within the second intron of RPP7. The use of both sites is reciprocally sensitive to FPA activity, with a moderate decrease in fpa-8 and an increase in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data.

claims.claim: Three alternative poly(A) sites located in the terminal intron of RPP7 were found, in addition to the previously reported most distal and most commonly used poly(A) site in the terminal exon (Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013).
claims.source: At the 3′ end of RPP7, we found three alternative poly(A) sites located in the terminal intron, in addition to the previously reported most distal and most commonly used poly(A) site in the terminal exon (Figure 6A, Inset 1) (Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 6A, Inset 1, and a citation to Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013.

claims.claim: Termination at the 3′UTR intronic poly(A) sites in RPP7 is suppressed by FPA: their usage is increased in fpa-8 and decreased in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.source: Termination at the 3′UTR intronic poly(A) sites is suppressed by FPA: their usage is increased in fpa-8 and decreased in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data.

claims.claim: Three poly(A) sites within protein-coding exon 6 of RPP7 were identified: two at the end of the region encoding the NB-ARC domain and one within the region encoding the LRR repeats.
claims.source: The major effect of FPA on RPP7 is within protein-coding exon 6, where we identified three poly(A) sites (Figure 6A, Inset 2): two at the end of the region encoding the NB-ARC domain and one within the region encoding the LRR repeats.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 6A, Inset 2.

claims.claim: Cleavage and polyadenylation at the exon 6 poly(A) sites in RPP7 result in transcripts without in-frame stop codons, thereby disrupting the coding potential of RPP7 mRNA.
claims.source: Cleavage and polyadenylation at these sites result in transcripts without in-frame stop codons, thereby disrupting the coding potential of RPP7 mRNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the Nanopore and Helicos DRS data showing poly(A) sites in exon 6.

claims.claim: In Col-0, 25% of RPP7 Nanopore DRS reads terminate at one of the exon 6 poly(A) sites; when FPA is overexpressed, this figure increases to 63%.
claims.source: The relative selection of exon 6 poly(A) sites depends on FPA expression: in Col-0, 25% of RPP7 Nanopore DRS reads terminate at one of these exon 6 poly(A) sites; and when FPA is overexpressed, this figure increases to 63%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: Only 23% of RPP7 transcripts are expected to encode RPP7 protein in the FPA-overexpressing line.
claims.source: Consequently, only 23% of RPP7 transcripts are expected to encode RPP7 protein in the FPA-overexpressing line.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the Nanopore DRS data showing increased exon 6 polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP.

claims.claim: In fpa-8, 4% of RPP7 Nanopore DRS reads terminate in exon 6, and 79% of transcripts are expected to be protein coding.
claims.source: In contrast, 4% of RPP7 Nanopore DRS reads identified in fpa-8 terminate in exon 6, and 79% of transcripts are expected to be protein coding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claims.claim: RNA gel blot analysis detected a clear decrease in signal corresponding to full-length RPP7 transcripts in 35S::FPA:YFP.
claims.source: In an orthogonal approach, we used RNA gel blot analysis to visualise RPP7 mRNAs in Col-0, fpa-8, and 35S::FPA:YFP backgrounds and detected a clear decrease in signal corresponding to full-length RPP7 transcripts in 35S::FPA:YFP (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA gel blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: RPP7 function is required for immunity to Hpa-Hiks1 in Col-0 (McDowell et al., 2000).
claims.source: RPP7 function is required for immunity to Hpa-Hiks1 in Col-0 (McDowell et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McDowell et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The Keswick (Ksk-1) accession is susceptible to Hpa-Hiks1 (Lai et al., 2019).

results.result: FPA co-purifies with proteins involved in mRNA 3′ end processing and transcription termination. IVI-MS identified 203 FPA co-purifying proteins, including 14 cleavage and polyadenylation factors (CPFs), spliceosome components, both Pol II subunits, kinases/phosphatases that modify Pol II CTD, and the exonuclease XRN3.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 are supported by IVI-MS data with appropriate controls (Col-0 vs 35S::FPA:YFP) and three biological replicates. The identification of CPFs, Pol II-associated factors, and transcription termination machinery is consistent with FPA's proposed role in 3′ end processing. The enrichment criteria (median log2 fold change >2) and validation by orthogonal RNA-binding proteome analysis strengthen the findings.

results.result: FPA is enriched at the 3′ end of genes and co-localizes with Pol II phosphorylated at Ser2 of the CTD. ChIP-Seq shows strong correlation between FPA and Pol II Ser2 occupancy (Spearman's ρ = 0.67, p<2×10⁻³⁰⁸), and FPA is required for proper Pol II Ser2 distribution at PIF5.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by ChIP-Seq data showing FPA enrichment at 3′ ends and strong statistical correlation with Pol II Ser2. The PIF5 example provides functional validation. The metagene analysis and genome-wide correlation provide robust evidence for FPA's association with transcription termination machinery.

results.result: FPA predominantly controls poly(A) site selection genome-wide. Using three orthogonal RNA sequencing technologies (Nanopore DRS, Helicos DRS, Illumina RNA-Seq), the authors show that loss of FPA function leads to distal poly(A) site selection (77.9-79.0% of affected loci), while FPA overexpression promotes proximal poly(A) site selection (56.7-75.3% of affected loci). Reciprocal regulation was observed at 16-44 loci depending on the technology.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C42 and C102 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from three independent sequencing technologies with appropriate replicates (3-6 biological replicates per technology). The reciprocal patterns in fpa-8 vs 35S::FPA:YFP provide strong evidence for FPA's direct role in poly(A) site choice. Statistical significance is demonstrated (hypergeometric tests, FDR corrections), and the overlap between technologies (39.6-44.0%) is reasonable given technical differences. The EMD metric appropriately accounts for both abundance and distance of poly(A) sites.

results.result: Illumina RNA-Seq identified 2535 loci with differential RNA processing in fpa-8 and 1747 loci in 35S::FPA:YFP, with most changes representing upregulation in fpa-8 (consistent with readthrough) and both up- and downregulation in 35S::FPA:YFP (consistent with proximal polyadenylation).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by Illumina RNA-Seq data with six biological replicates and appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR < 0.05, absolute logFC >1). The patterns of differential expression are consistent with the proposed mechanisms of FPA action. However, the annotation-agnostic approach and the large number of affected loci suggest some findings may be indirect effects.

results.result: FPA does not influence global levels of mRNA m6A methylation, despite components of the m6A writer complex co-purifying with FPA.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis showing no difference in m6A/A ratios between Col-0, fpa-8, and 35S::FPA:YFP, with vir-1 serving as a positive control. This negative result is important for ruling out an indirect mechanism and distinguishing plant FPA from its human/Drosophila homologs.

results.result: FPA-dependent poly(A) site choice is not an indirect consequence of FPA control of IBM1. Only 10.6% of loci with altered poly(A) site choice in 35S::FPA:YFP have altered H3K9me2 in ibm1 mutants (hypergeometric p=0.97).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by analysis of two independent H3K9me2 ChIP-Seq datasets in ibm1 mutants. The lack of significant overlap (hypergeometric p=0.97) argues against an indirect mechanism through IBM1-mediated chromatin changes. This is an important control for ruling out a major confounding pathway.

results.result: NLR-associated protein domains (NB-ARC, Rx-like CC, LRR) are enriched among loci with increased proximal polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by protein domain enrichment analysis using InterPro annotations on both Nanopore and Helicos DRS datasets. The enrichment analysis appropriately uses permutation testing to assess significance. This finding establishes NLRs as major targets of FPA regulation.

results.result: Long-read Nanopore DRS enables correction of NLR gene annotations. AT5G46490 is actually a single locus with a 2.7 kb intron (not two separate genes), and RPS6 has a complex 3′UTR that overlaps with a previously unannotated gene encoding an RPS6-like TIR domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by Nanopore DRS data showing full-length transcripts that span previously mis-annotated gene boundaries. The reannotations are corroborated by nanoPARE data showing capped 5′ ends. These findings demonstrate the value of long-read sequencing for resolving complex NLR loci and have implications for understanding RPS6-dependent autoimmunity.

results.result: Half (50%) of expressed NLR genes show FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation. FPA-sensitive NLRs are significantly enriched in major gene clusters (59.5%, chi²p=0.02) and among NLRs under high diversifying selection (71.4%, chi²p=0.02), suggesting association with rapidly evolving NLRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are supported by systematic analysis of 124 expressed NLRs using Nanopore DRS with manual curation. The statistical associations with gene clusters and diversifying selection are significant, though the association with synteny diversity is not (p=0.09). The high proportion of FPA-sensitive NLRs (50%) is a major finding, though the manual curation approach may introduce some subjectivity.

results.result: FPA controls readthrough and chimeric RNA formation at 17 NLR genes. Examples include increased readthrough into downstream TEs at AT1G58848/AT1G59218 in fpa-8, and chimeric RNA formation between AT1G63730 and AT1G63740 in fpa-8.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by Nanopore DRS and Helicos DRS data showing readthrough transcripts and chimeric RNAs. The AT1G63730-AT1G63740 chimera is statistically significant (Helicos EMD = 1099, FDR = 0.02). However, the functional consequences of these chimeric RNAs are not tested.

results.result: FPA controls intronic polyadenylation at 17 NLR genes. At AT1G69550, a proximal poly(A) site in intron 3 produces transcripts encoding a protein lacking most of the LRR domain; readthrough at this site is increased in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 1271, FDR = 1.2×10⁻⁴).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by Nanopore DRS data showing intronic poly(A) sites and statistical analysis of their usage. The AT1G69550 example is well-documented with significant changes in fpa-8. However, the functional consequences of the truncated protein are not tested.

results.result: FPA controls premature termination within protein-coding exons at 45 NLR genes, producing stop-codonless transcripts. At RPP28, multiple exonic poly(A) sites were detected with reciprocal regulation by FPA (Helicos EMD = 859-912, FDR < 10⁻⁸). At AT5G40060, exonic polyadenylation produces a transcript that may encode a TIR-only protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data showing exonic poly(A) sites with strong statistical significance. The stop-codonless nature of these transcripts is inferred from the data and is consistent with non-stop decay targeting. The AT5G40060 example involving a uORF is well-reasoned but the translation efficiency and protein production are not experimentally validated.

results.result: At seven NLR genes, exonic proximal polyadenylation is associated with upstream intron retention. At RPS4, intron 3 retention in 35S::FPA:YFP is associated with proximal polyadenylation in exon 4 (Helicos EMD = 34, not significant).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are partially supported. While Nanopore DRS shows the association between intron retention and exonic polyadenylation at seven genes, the RPS4 example is not statistically significant (EMD = 34, not significant). The mechanistic link between intron retention and polyadenylation is inferred but not directly tested. Additional validation would strengthen this result.

results.result: FPA controls complex alternative polyadenylation at RPP4, including chimeric RNA formation with downstream TE AT4G16870, cryptic splicing producing TIR-domain-only transcripts, and intronic proximal polyadenylation. Loss of FPA decreases chimeric RNA formation, while FPA overexpression increases intronic proximal polyadenylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 are supported by convergent evidence from Nanopore DRS, Helicos DRS, and Illumina RNA-Seq showing multiple modes of FPA-dependent regulation at RPP4. The cryptic splicing event producing TIR-only transcripts is particularly well-documented. However, the functional consequences of these different transcript isoforms are not tested.

results.result: FPA controls RPP7 expression through multiple mechanisms, with the major effect being premature termination in protein-coding exon 6. Three poly(A) sites in exon 6 produce stop-codonless transcripts; their usage increases from 25% in Col-0 to 63% in 35S::FPA:YFP, reducing protein-coding transcripts from 77% to 23%. RNA gel blot analysis confirms decreased full-length RPP7 transcripts in 35S::FPA:YFP.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C92 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from Nanopore DRS, Helicos DRS, and RNA gel blot analysis. The quantification of transcript isoforms is based on read counts and is consistent across technologies. The RNA gel blot provides orthogonal validation of decreased full-length transcripts. This is a comprehensive characterization of FPA's effect on a single NLR gene.

results.result: FPA overexpression compromises RPP7-dependent immunity to Hpa-Hiks1. While Col-0, fpa-7, and fpa-8 are resistant (median: 0 sporangiophores), 35S::FPA:YFP plants show significantly increased susceptibility (median: 3 sporangiophores, p=3.8×10⁻⁹ vs pFPA::FPA control).
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C101 are supported by pathogenesis assays with appropriate controls (Col-0, Ksk-1, fpa-7, fpa-8, pFPA::FPA) across three independent experiments. The statistical analysis using negative binomial regression is appropriate for count data. The result demonstrates functional consequences of FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation. However, the mechanism linking reduced full-length RPP7 transcripts to compromised immunity is inferred rather than directly demonstrated (e.g., through RPP7 protein quantification or complementation).

results.result: Widespread premature transcription termination of NLR genes by FPA has functional consequences for immunity. Half of expressed NLRs are sensitive to FPA, with FPA predominantly promoting exonic polyadenylation. At RPP7, increased exonic polyadenylation by FPA overexpression compromises immunity to Hpa-Hiks1.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 synthesize the major findings and are supported by the combined evidence from genome-wide analysis (50% of NLRs affected) and functional validation at RPP7. The conclusion that transcription termination plays an important role in NLR regulation and evolution is well-supported, though the evolutionary implications are somewhat speculative.

results.result: Components of the m6A writer complex co-purify with FPA, but unlike related proteins in human and Drosophila, FPA is not required to maintain global levels of m6A modification in Arabidopsis.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by IVI-MS data showing co-purification and LC-MS/MS data showing no change in m6A levels. This distinguishes plant FPA from its animal homologs and rules out an indirect mechanism through m6A modification.

results.result: FPA specifically interacts with CID-containing PCF11 paralogs (PCFS2, PCFS4) but not CID-lacking paralogs (PCFS1, PCFS5), suggesting FPA controls alternative polyadenylation by altering Pol II speed and transcription termination.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by IVI-MS data showing selective co-purification. The mechanistic interpretation is reasonable given the known functions of PCF11 CID domains in transcription termination, but remains inferential. Direct tests of Pol II elongation rate or termination efficiency would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The FPA SPOC domain may interact with Pol II CTD, possibly in conjunction with CID domains of PCFS2 and PCFS4, based on conservation of electropositive patches with the human SPOC domain protein PHF3.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by citations to structural studies, but C114 is speculative. The conservation of one electropositive patch suggests possible CTD interaction, but this is not experimentally tested. Direct binding assays or structural studies would be needed to support this model.

results.result: Long-read Nanopore DRS reveals that RPS6 is transcribed through a previously unrecognized downstream gene encoding an RPS6-like TIR domain, and expression of this gene is dependent on the RNA exosome component HEN2, which suppresses RPS6-dependent autoimmune phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 are supported by Nanopore DRS data showing the novel TIR-encoding gene and its dependence on HEN2. The connection to RPS6-dependent autoimmunity is supported by citation to Takagi et al., 2020. This finding provides important context for understanding RPS6-mediated autoimmunity, though the functional role of the TIR-only protein is not directly tested.

results.result: FPA controls NLR 3′ end formation through three mechanisms: (i) preventing readthrough in 3′UTRs, (ii) promoting intronic polyadenylation, and (iii) promoting exonic polyadenylation producing stop-codonless transcripts. These mechanisms have diverse consequences including NMD targeting, production of protein isoforms (e.g., TIR-only proteins), and altered 3′UTR biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C128 synthesize the findings and are supported by the combined data from multiple NLR genes. The three modes of regulation are well-documented. The consequences are largely inferred from known biology (e.g., NMD targeting of long 3′UTRs, functions of TIR-only proteins) rather than directly tested in this study, but the inferences are reasonable and supported by citations.

results.result: Alternative polyadenylation may enable dynamic regulation of NLR expression during pathogen surveillance vs. infection, facilitate rapid NLR evolution while reducing autoimmunity, contribute to cryptic genetic variation, and directly facilitate neofunctionalization through chimeric RNA formation and retrotransposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C134 are largely speculative models for the evolutionary and regulatory significance of FPA-dependent NLR regulation. While the models are plausible and supported by citations to relevant literature, they are not directly tested in this study. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work rather than established results.

results.result: FPA-dependent exonic termination at RPP7 is conserved across the RPP7 locus and may modulate hybrid necrosis by limiting expression of RPP7-like proteins and HR4. FPA also controls DM10, which can cause autoimmunity when truncated, suggesting FPA overexpression could trigger autoimmune phenotypes in some genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 are supported by data showing FPA regulation of multiple RPP7-like genes. Claims C137-C142 are supported by citations to hybrid necrosis studies. However, C140 and C142 are speculative - the potential for FPA to rescue or trigger autoimmunity in specific genetic backgrounds is not tested. These are reasonable hypotheses but require experimental validation.

results.result: RNA-binding protein-dependent modulation of NLR expression may be a general phenomenon (supported by CPSF30 suppression of autoimmunity) and could be targeted by pathogen effectors (as seen with HopU1 targeting AtGRP7 and Pi4089 targeting StKRBP1). This mechanism might explain quantitative disease resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C151 are supported by citations showing that other RNA-binding proteins affect NLR regulation and that pathogen effectors can target RNA-binding proteins. However, the extension to FPA as a potential effector target and the link to quantitative disease resistance are speculative. These are interesting hypotheses but not directly tested.

results.result: Long-read Nanopore DRS provides superior insight into NLR complexity compared to short-read technologies. The EMD metric appropriately captures both abundance and distance of poly(A) sites. A combined approach using long-read sequencing to generate bespoke annotations for short-read analysis is valuable until long-read throughput matches short-read technologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 are supported by the comparative analysis of three sequencing technologies and the successful application of the EMD metric. The methodological insights are well-demonstrated through the reannotation of complex NLR loci and the complementary strengths of different technologies. The recommendation for combined approaches is practical and well-justified.

results.result: Premature transcription termination of NLR genes is widespread (50% of expressed NLRs). Nanopore DRS improved NLR annotation accuracy and revealed a layer of regulation that may influence NLR evolution. Continued development of full-length RNA sequencing approaches will likely reveal other important aspects of biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 are supported by the systematic analysis of NLR genes and the successful reannotation of complex loci. C161 is a reasonable extrapolation based on the success of the approach. These claims effectively summarize the major contributions of the study.
